article.overview: A regolith processing experiment tests whether useful products, such as oxygen, water, metals or construction feedstock, can be extracted from lunar regolith, the loose layer of broken rock and dust that covers the Moon's surface. It belongs to in-situ resource utilisation (ISRU), in which a mission makes some of what it needs from local material rather than launching every consumable from Earth. The sources reviewed for this article describe laboratory, simulant-based and breadboard work. They do not describe a lunar-surface regolith experiment that has produced oxygen on the Moon. The nearest flown oxygen-production analogue is MOXIE, which operated on Mars using the atmosphere rather than regolith [4].
article.description: Regolith processing experiment is a broad catalogue name rather than one standard instrument. Designs differ in the chemistry they use. Molten regolith electrolysis melts regolith and passes an electric current through it [2]. Carbothermal reduction uses carbon-based reactants or concentrated sunlight at very high temperatures to release oxygen from oxides [3]. Hydrogen reduction reacts hydrogen with ilmenite to form water [5]. Most experiments also need subsystems for feeding and metering regolith, handling hot material, removing waste slag, and collecting and measuring the gases produced. The defining feature is the processing step: the experiment transforms regolith and then measures the product, rather than only analysing a sample.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose is to find out whether regolith-based production works reliably enough to support later missions. Key measurements include the mass of product per hour, the energy needed per unit of product, product purity, the fraction of the oxygen in the feed that is actually recovered, and how yield changes with regolith composition. Applications include oxygen for breathing and as a rocket oxidiser, water for drinking and for splitting into hydrogen and oxygen, metals and feedstock for construction, and verification of processes before crewed or large-scale use. NASA states that post-test analysis of the 2024 molten regolith electrolysis test will help teams understand the thermal and chemical function of full-scale reactors for the lunar surface [1]. The reviewed evidence is about process performance; it does not yet show operation in a lunar environment.
article.operating_principle: Oxygen on the Moon is mostly locked in oxide minerals within regolith, so extraction means breaking those chemical bonds. In molten regolith electrolysis, the regolith is heated until it is molten and an electric current drives oxygen ions to an anode, where oxygen gas forms; metals are reduced at the cathode. This is a general description of the process, not a reported result of the cited test. The 2024 Kennedy test sustained continuous electrolysis for nine hours, with Joule heating keeping the regolith molten, and measured oxygen with a gas-analysis system [2]. Carbothermal reduction heats regolith to very high temperatures so that carbon can strip oxygen from the oxides; Sierra Space's reactor concentrates sunlight on the regolith, and the unmelted regolith insulates the molten material so that thermal control is passive [3]. Hydrogen reduction reacts hydrogen with ilmenite, an iron-titanium oxide, at roughly 700 to 1000 °C to form water, iron and titanium dioxide [5]. The Mars instrument MOXIE used a different route, solid oxide electrolysis of carbon dioxide at about 800 °C [4].
article.scientific_importance: Regolith processing matters because it could reduce how much mass must be launched from Earth. Oxygen is a large share of the propellant and life-support requirements in most mission concepts, and carrying it from Earth is expensive. Regolith-based oxygen is only useful if it can be extracted in quantity, reliably, from realistic material. Recent results show progress at laboratory and prototype scale, including a 25 kg molten regolith electrolysis test and a fully automated solar carbothermal reactor tested in vacuum [1][2][3]. They do not yet demonstrate continuous lunar-surface operation, and the yield of any process depends on the composition of the local regolith.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a regolith processing experiment, because the payload class spans chemically different processes, power levels and hardware scales. The examples below describe specific tested, flown or proposed systems. Where a value is not published in the sources reviewed, it is marked as not verified (null) rather than estimated. The values are not directly comparable: a flown Mars instrument, a laboratory reactor and a breadboard test differ in purpose, scale and environment.

examples.name: MOXIE (Mars Oxygen ISRU Experiment)
examples.type: Flown Mars ISRU oxygen-production instrument (not a lunar payload)
examples.status: Flown on Mars, Perseverance rover, 2021 to 2023
examples.description: Produced oxygen from the Martian atmosphere by solid oxide electrolysis of carbon dioxide at about 800 °C [4]. Included because it is the only flown ISRU oxygen-production instrument identified in the sources reviewed.
examples.run_average_rate_g_per_hour_reviewer_cal: approximately 5.5 to 5.9 (calculated from Table 1 of the 2022 paper; not stated by the authors)

examples.name: LR-1 molten regolith electrolysis test (Lunar Resources Inc. reactor at NASA Kennedy Space Center)
examples.type: Laboratory molten regolith electrolysis test (simulant, vacuum chamber)
examples.status: Laboratory test in late 2024; not flown; not on the Moon
examples.description: Molten regolith electrolysis of lunar regolith simulant in a Kennedy vacuum chamber retrofitted to simulate relevant environment conditions. Electrolysis was sustained for nine hours with Joule heating keeping the regolith molten. A custom gas-measurement system (VMOMS) monitored production in real time. NASA describes this as the first time it had produced molecular oxygen with this process [1][2].
examples.metal_production: Claimed in a company press release (iron and silicon); not confirmed in the NASA conference abstract, which names oxygen as the only product identified. Treated as unconfirmed.

examples.name: Carbothermal Oxygen Production Reactor (COPR), Sierra Space
examples.status: Not flown; thermal-vacuum testing at NASA Johnson Space Center in summer 2024; integration testing under NASA CaRD planned for summer 2025
examples.description: Heats lunar regolith simulant directly with concentrated solar energy. The unmelted regolith insulates the molten material, giving passive thermal control. Automated handling meters, weighs and feeds regolith and removes reduced metallic slag. The paper states that hardware maturity reached TRL 6 and that oxygen-extraction energy efficiency and production yield exceeded program goals.

examples.name: ProSPA hydrogen-reduction breadboards (Open University, ilmenite and regolith)
examples.type: Laboratory breadboard hydrogen-reduction instrument concept; proposed lunar-surface experiment
examples.status: Laboratory breadboard; planned lunar-surface experiment as part of ESA's PROSPECT package; mission schedule uncertain (sources disagree); not flown
examples.description: Static-system hydrogen reduction breadboards producing water and oxygen from ilmenite. A regolith-type PhD thesis from the same group reported an average yield of about 0.94 wt% O2. Figures come from search-result summaries and should be checked against the full-text papers.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The MOXIE chassis measures 23.9 cm by 23.9 cm by 30.9 cm [4]. No dimensions are verified for the LR-1 reactor, the COPR reactor or any lunar-scale regolith processing unit. Dimensions for a future system would be set by its feed rate, reactor size, thermal insulation and the need to package gas handling and regolith handling within a lander's envelope. The examples above are not comparable in size because they are laboratory, flight-like and breadboard systems.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The MOXIE instrument mass is not stated in the 2022 Science Advances paper [4]. The LR-1 reactor mass, the COPR mass and the ProSPA breadboard mass are not verified in the sources reviewed. Mass would be a key constraint for lander delivery, and no lunar-scale unit mass is assumed in this article.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power for the processes is substantial in principle, because molten regolith electrolysis uses Joule heating and electrolysis, and carbothermal reduction needs very high temperatures. No verified power value was found for the LR-1 reactor, the COPR reactor or a lunar-scale unit. MOXIE's power is not stated in the 2022 paper [4]. The COPR concept uses concentrated solar energy as its heat source [3], which would need an approved power and solar-concentrator arrangement.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: Regolith processing reactors must operate in vacuum, with lunar day and night thermal cycling, abrasive dust and hot, reactive material. Molten regolith electrolysis and carbothermal reduction both require very high process temperatures; the Kennedy test and the COPR reactor are reported at these conditions [2][3]. The processes need substantial energy for heating and electrolysis, and no verified lunar-scale power value was found in the sources reviewed. Operation would also require thermal management, controlled regolith feed, handling of hot slag and gas, dust control, and a reliable gas-measurement or product-collection system. Hydrogen-reduction concepts additionally need a hydrogen supply, which is not produced on site in the reviewed demonstrations [5]. Ilmenite content strongly affects yield, and one source suggests ilmenite concentrations in high-latitude regions may be below 1%, which would give low oxygen yields [5]. These requirements are engineering considerations; they are not a certified design specification for any payload.
article.limitations: The evidence is laboratory-scale. The reviewed oxygen-production results come from simulants, milligram-scale samples or prototype reactors, not from a flown lunar experiment [1][2][3][5]. Yield depends strongly on composition. A 2026 arXiv study concludes that oxygen extraction in realistic regolith is governed by the response of the whole regolith rather than ilmenite content alone, which matters for low-ilmenite highland and polar material [7]. The hydrogen-reduction yields reported in small samples are low, at about 1 wt% oxygen [5]. Metal co-production is unconfirmed. Long-term durability over many cycles, and power, mass and thermal management at lunar scale, are not demonstrated. MOXIE showed resistance growth with heating and cooling cycles and expects more than 60 cycles, but its authors state that long-term durability and resilience remain to be demonstrated [4].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A regolith processing unit would be delivered to the Moon as a surface payload integrated into a lander's payload compartment or an attached package. Its reactor, regolith feed and handling, gas-measurement and thermal subsystems would need to fit launch constraints. No mass or dimensions for a lunar-scale unit are verified, so packaging volume cannot be stated.
transportation_process: Integrate the reactor, regolith feed and handling, gas-measurement and thermal subsystems into a lander's payload compartment or attached package on Earth.
Launch the lander on a launch vehicle.
Deliver the payload to the surface using a lander.
Place the reactor on a stable, level surface and connect power and data.
Set up regolith intake and gas-sampling lines, then commission the process.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The method could be robotic or crewed. No deployment method is verified for a specific system. Sierra Space's COPR concept relies on concentrated solar energy and would need a solar-concentrator and power arrangement that has not been verified for any lander [3]. Molten regolith electrolysis requires significant electrical power for heating and electrolysis [2].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: No lunar-surface regolith processing experiment has been flown in the sources reviewed. The MOXIE instrument operated on Mars aboard the Perseverance rover from 2021 to 2023 [4][6]. Its lunar relevance is as an analogue for ISRU oxygen production, not as a lunar deployment precedent.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Compatibility with a named lander, rover or spacecraft is not assessed, because no verified interface evidence was found for any regolith processing system. Mass, dimensions, power, thermal interface, regolith-handling interface and deployment method would each need to be checked against verified spacecraft specifications before any lander is named.

article.historical_significance: MOXIE, which operated on Mars from 2021 to 2023, is widely described as the first demonstration of ISRU on another planet [4][6]. It showed that solid oxide electrolysis of atmospheric carbon dioxide can produce oxygen on a planetary surface. For the Moon, the most significant recent result is NASA's first production of molecular oxygen by molten regolith electrolysis at laboratory scale, using a 25 kg simulant batch in 2024 [1][2]. Carbothermal and hydrogen-reduction work has advanced the technology base, but none of the reviewed lunar results is a flight demonstration.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The term regolith processing experiment describes a class of work, so the figures above describe distinct systems that should not be combined or compared directly. The following items remain unverified: the LR-1 reactor's mass, power and vacuum pressure; the company claim of metal production; the COPR numerical yield and energy efficiency, because the full PDF could not be read; the ProSPA mission status and schedule; the difference between the MOXIE 2022 paper totals and the later reported 122 g total; and any lunar-surface power or mass values. The ProSPA figures rely on search-result summaries rather than full-text review, and the Open University record page could not be retrieved directly. A solar pyrolysis oxygen test reported in secondary coverage was not included because its figures could not be verified. No direct image asset URL was verified for this payload, so the article contains no embedded images. Lunar location recommendations are excluded, as instructed.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values are absent because no image was verified. All reference and source URLs in this file have query strings and fragments removed.

data_quality_notes: No direct image asset URL was verified from an official page in this run, so no images are included. Image arrays are empty by design rather than populated with unverified URLs.
COPR numerical yield and energy efficiency are null: the NASA ICES-2025 abstract states that they exceeded program goals but gives no values, and the full PDF could not be read (binary content).
The LR-1 metal-production claim (iron and silicon) comes from a company press release and is not confirmed by the NASA abstract, which identifies oxygen as the only product.

MOXIE totals differ by source: the 2022 Science Advances paper reports 49.9 g over seven 2021 runs, and later secondary reporting of NASA statements gives 122 g over 16 runs with a best rate of 12 g per hour. The later figures were not confirmed against a primary NASA page.

ProSPA figures (45 mg, 0.3 mmol, 850 to 1050 C, 11.2 mg sample at 1.4 wt% O2, regolith average 0.94 wt% O2) come from search-result summaries; the Open University record and full text returned HTTP 403, so they were not checked against the papers. Mission schedule differs between sources and is not assumed.
A solar pyrolysis oxygen experiment reported in secondary coverage was excluded because its figures could not be verified.
The arXiv 2601.14719 reference is used only for a general composition finding, from a search-result summary; the full text was not read.
Research budget used: 7 WebSearch calls and 7 page reads; three reads failed (HTTP 403 for the Open University and core.ac.uk pages, and binary PDF content for the COPR paper).
